source_title: Corsair Voxara USB Gaming Condenser Microphone Review
source_excerpt:
The bar for a good enough gaming mic is pretty low these days. Plenty of gaming headsets ship with totally serviceable mics off the bat, and it's hard to recommend a good deal of standalone gaming USB microphones because, beyond the RGB lights and cool-factor markup, they offer too small a quality bump for the price. Yet after spending some time with the Corsair Voxara , the company's first-ever premium USB condenser microphone, I can't help but be impressed. For a first attempt at a gaming mic at "studio quality," this is a stylish and shockingly strong performer that does a lot to earn its price point.
It's also a very modern offering, as the Corsair Voxara largely makes its case by pairing substantial Corsair hardware with Elgato's Wave Link 3.0 software and capitalizing on the increasing prevalence of gaming and streaming tools. After a week of daily use and testing in an untreated home office, that's actually what has earned the Voxara a permanent spot on my desk. It may not compete well against more professional studio microphones, but it doesn't really need to; Corsair's goal was to push the upper limits of what a gaming microphone can offer at this price point, and by that metric, it largely succeeds.
Corsair Voxara microphone with integrated shock mount
1/4" to 5/8" and 3/8" to 5/8" thread adapters
Frankly, the unboxing process is rather to the point, but simplicity here is certainly no crime. The essentials are all here, and two thread adapters stand as a more thoughtful inclusion, since the Voxara's native 5/8" thread means it should fit nearly any boom arm without a trip to the store. The cable is non-braided, a small miss at this price, but at 10 feet it reaches comfortably across most desk layouts.
Setup is also essentially plug-and-play. My PC recognized the Voxara as soon as I connected it, and installing Wave Link to unlock its full feature set added only a few minutes on top of that. To make the most of the microphone, though, download the Elgato Equalizer add-on from the Wave Link Marketplace as well — that'll add further EQ customization and even downloadable presets to make things even easier.
The Voxara is about as good a blend of form and function as this category offers. The sharply designed PC+ABS body sits on a hefty aluminum stand with 360-degree rotation and about 30 degrees of tilt; it looks premium, but it's subtler than most, despite the lights. It comes in black or white, and the customizable RGB on the mic cycles between a multicolor pattern, a solid color, and a very nice level meter mode that doubles as a real-time visual gain indicator.
The onboard controls aren't flashy, but the components are excellent, and they do everything they need to: the front wheel scrolls infinitely and clicks to cycle between mic gain, headphone volume, and side tone balance. While holding the wheel for two seconds flips the display for upside-down boom arm mounting. A small OLED screen solves the classic infinite-dial problem, since you always know exactly where your levels sit, and it also displays the current value and mute status at all times. The rear knob handles RGB modes, and you can press it to cycle sub-modes if you make any through Wave Link, but the nifty tap-to-mute ring up top is the clear standout here, as it's both stylish and remarkably responsive.
The only real build complaint concerns the stand: the integrated shock mount helps, but the heavy aluminum base still passes along vibrations from harder desk bumps. That's par for the course with desk stands, though, and a boom arm is, frankly, the right call for any microphone. And, to Corsair's credit, the shock-mounted body is the part that attaches to arms, which makes the upgrade painless.
Frequency Response: 20 Hz – 20,000 Hz
The Corsair Voxara's 25mm condenser capsule and 32-bit/192kHz audio engine are what truly deliver on the studio-grade promise Corsair has made with this microphone. As someone who has spent years behind microphones, I found its sound warmer and more detailed than most, even from close to two feet away, with none of the thin, boxy quality that plagues many gaming mics. The cardioid pickup pattern does a solid job of prioritizing the voice in front of it, too.
In an office with no acoustic treatment whatsoever, the raw signal still carries some room character, but that's a job the software handles well (more on that later). Plosives are the Voxara's most noticeable weakness, but I'm not sure if I can name any mic with a built-in pop-filter that handles them any better. The bar in this hard-shell mic market is admittedly low, and anyone sensitive to plosives will still want an external pop filter.
While this is its own section, it's important to note that the second half of the Voxara's appeal is its software integration with Elgato's Wave Link 3.0. That's important because Voxara has no onboard signal processing, so effects run on your computer instead. That puts a bit more load on your system, but it also means more control, and many users (myself included) will prefer it that way.
It also helps that Wave Link might be the best-branded software in this niche of the market, occupying the perfect middle ground between user-friendliness and customization. Wave Link asks a little more of the user up front and pays that back with much deeper options over time, handling routing firsthand and going deeper on compression and effects than most, thanks to the Elgato Marketplace, which allows for EQ mixing, presets, and even voice filters — though some of the more grandiose stuff comes with a price tag.
The Corsair Voxara also supports iCUE Murals through iCUE Apps for RGB syncing, though that's still in beta.
The most intuitive and impressive feature is Voice Focus, as this flavor of AI-powered noise suppression just works so well out of the gate. Having tested all kinds of AI noise suppression, this is by far the best implementation I've used to date, and in my untreated office, its lowest setting on the Weak-to-Strong slider was perfect, cutting room noise without coloring my voice. The Voxara does skip some features other recent mics have introduced, such as voice tracking and onboard presets, but it loses color more than depth, and what the Voxara does, makes up for it.
Compatibility-wise, the Corsair Voxara connects via USB-C to both Windows and macOS, as well as PS4, PS5, Nintendo Switch, and Switch 2. It's important to note, though, that Wave Link only runs on PC and Mac, so console players will get the raw capsule without Voice Focus or EQ. Thankfully, the raw signal sounds good on its own, and should any adjustment be needed, a 3.5mm headphone jack handles monitoring, with side tone balance adjustable right from the front wheel.
Ultimately, the Corsair Voxara is a very solid microphone; it's one of the few premier, standalone USB gaming mics that justifies its 199.99 price tag. Of course, that price will be unnecessary or out of reach for plenty of gamers, and anyone who only needs to be heard in voice chat can do just fine for much less. But for players who care how they sound, or who want a mic that can handle streaming, content creation, or the occasional professional recording, the Voxara is an easy recommendation.
It may not be the best mic for working professionals, it isn't an XLR, and it doesn't chase the biggest screen or the longest feature list. But it's truly studio-grade, it is pretty, and it seems rare for a mic in this corner of the market to manage both without anything getting stuck with the bill. It offers plenty of substance per dollar compared to much of the competition at this price, and combined with how much Wave Link adds on top, I'm pleasantly surprised to say the Corsair Voxara is one of the more impressive mics I've encountered in its niche.
The Corsair Voxara is currently available for $199.99 USD on Corsair's website . GameRant was provided a unit for this review.
